newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: Ivorian 1st half Nov cocoa arrivals 130-175,000 T.
newsitem.headline: Ivorian 1st half Nov cocoa arrivals 130-175,000 T.

text.p: Estimates of cocoa arrivals in Ivory Coast in the first half of November vary widely, ranging from just over 130,000 tonnes up to 175,000 tonnes, exporters and upcountry sources say.

But buyers in the second port of San Pedro, which is catching up with Abidjan for cocoa exports, said things there had slowed, with comparatively little arriving, and mould was a problem with some of the cocoa that had arrived.

In a market characterised by conflicting signals it was not immediately clear just how much cocoa was waiting upcountry for transport to the ports, but one buyer near Daloa said about one third of what had been there had been shifted.
"It's very, very quiet -- the calm before the storm," said a San-Pedro based exporter.
"Nothing is going on at all. It's coming in drop by drop," said another. Mould suggested upcountry drying problems but bean size was excellent.
But one Abidjan-based analyst said up-country evacuation of pods had been booming and declared arrivals in both ports on November 10 stood at 175,000 tonnes.

Other estimates proved more conservative. One local trade source put arrivals at less than 132,000 tonnes up to November 15. Trade sources in Amsterdam were working on a figure of around 165,000 tonnes by November 10.
As a rule of thumb, arrivals of 250,000 tonnes by the end of November will confirm a main crop in excess of 900,000 tonnes and a likely total of around 1.05 million, forecasters say.
In the 1995/96 season, which totalled a record 1.2 million tonnes, a rush at the end of November caught forecasters by surprise and pushed the monthly figure over 300,000 tonnes.
A shipping rate dispute in 1995 slowed arrivals until mid-November, making comparisons with this year difficult, but San Pedro buyers thought a repeat of last season unlikely.
"Nobody really knows what is happening at present but we would be very, very surprised if it went up to 300,000 by the end of November like last year," one said.
